assertions.text: Fulfillment method splitting is represented as its own table — items with different fulfillment types (store pickup vs home delivery) cannot share a shipment.
assertions.evidence: Fulfillment type is a column in 'Order Split Groups' table mixed with availability and addresses. Expected output specifies five distinct tables, but response provides three, combining concerns.

assertions.text: Delivery address splitting is represented as its own table — items going to different addresses must be in separate shipments.
assertions.evidence: Delivery Addresses is a column in 'Order Split Groups' mixed with fulfillment type and availability. Expected five tables with each concern separate; response combines three concerns in one table.

assertions.text: Availability splitting is represented as its own table — in-stock items ship immediately, backordered/pre-ordered items ship when available.
assertions.evidence: Availability is a column in 'Order Split Groups' mixed with fulfillment and addresses. Expected structure calls for five distinct tables; response has only three tables mixing unrelated concerns.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation (minimising shipments) is represented as its own table — choosing which warehouses to ship from to minimise total shipment count.
assertions.evidence: Separate 'Warehouse Selection — Minimising Shipments' table dedicated to this concern with scenarios like 'Two-warehouse solution preferred over three'.

assertions.text: Companion product grouping is represented as its own table — paired items (e.g. camera body and lens) should ship together from the same location when possible.
assertions.evidence: Separate 'Companion Products — Keeping Items Together' table with 9 scenarios dedicated to companion pairing logic.

assertions.text: Fulfillment table covers at least: all items for home delivery, all items for store pickup, and a mix of delivery and pickup items.
assertions.evidence: Order Split Groups includes 'Simple order, all ready' (home only), 'All items for store pickup', and 'Pickup and delivery in same order' (mixed).

assertions.text: Delivery address table covers at least: all items to the same address, and items to different addresses.
assertions.evidence: Order Split Groups includes rows with 'Delivery Addresses: 1' (same address throughout) and 'Two delivery addresses, all in stock' plus 'Two delivery addresses, all deferred'.

assertions.text: Availability table covers at least: all items in stock, a mix of in-stock and pre-order/backorder, and two backordered/pre-ordered items with different dates. Pre-order and backorder are recognised as equivalent for splitting semantics — either by comment, note, or by including both with the same rules.
assertions.evidence: Covers all-stock ('Simple order, all ready'), mixes (In-stock + backordered rows), and different dates ('Both deferred but different dates, same destination: Backordered (week 2) + pre-order (week 6)').

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table covers at least: single warehouse has full quantity, multi-warehouse split needed, fewer-warehouse split preferred over more warehouses, and cannot fulfill (insufficient total stock).
assertions.evidence: Warehouse table includes 'Single warehouse fully satisfies', 'Two-warehouse solution preferred over three', 'Three warehouses required', and 'Insufficient total stock — cannot fulfill'.

assertions.text: Companion table covers at least: single warehouse has both companions, unavoidable split (no warehouse has both but both are available), and fulfillment not possible (one companion not available anywhere).
assertions.evidence: Nine scenarios in Companion table cover co-location and unavoidable split ('Companions only available at separate warehouses'), but no scenario shows one companion completely unavailable.

assertions.text: Scenario names describe the business situation (e.g. 'Consolidate: two beats three', 'Everything at one warehouse') — not 'Test case 2'.
assertions.evidence: All scenarios use descriptive business language: 'Simple order, all ready', 'Two-warehouse solution preferred over three', 'Non-companion only at a second warehouse'.

assertions.text: Trigger tables represent multi-item orders where each item has its own fulfillment type, address, and availability. The notation makes the item-to-property mapping unambiguous — not value sets like {delivery, pickup} which lose which item has which property.
assertions.evidence: Order Split Groups row 'Pickup and delivery in same order' shows 'Fulfillment Types: Home Delivery, Store Pickup' without mapping which items have which type. Ambiguous which item has pickup vs delivery.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table uses a scalar count column (e.g. 'Qty ordered') not item lists, when product identity doesn't matter for the logic.
assertions.evidence: Warehouse Selection table uses 'Quantity Needed' column with scalars: '6 shirts', '9 shirts', not itemized lists.

assertions.text: Column names use business/domain language (e.g. 'Shipments?' not 'Result?', 'Warehouse stock' not 'inventory_map'). The tables read as a specification a product person could review.
assertions.evidence: Uses 'Shipments?', 'Warehouse Inventory', 'Companions Together?', 'Fulfillment Types', 'Delivery Addresses' — all domain-appropriate language.

assertions.text: Output/expected columns end with '?' (e.g. 'Shipments?', 'Groups?') to distinguish them from input columns.
assertions.evidence: All output columns use question marks: 'Shipments?', 'Selected Warehouses?', 'Companions Together?', 'Split Reasons?'.

assertions.text: Inventory assignments are physically valid: items are only assigned to locations that have them. Shipment counts match the assignments shown.
assertions.evidence: Warehouse table example 'Two-warehouse solution (exact)' shows Philadelphia: 3 + Washington: 3 = 6 needed = 2 shipments. All assignments mathematically consistent and feasible.

assertions.text: Multiple open questions are surfaced across the tables — ambiguities, edge cases, or product decisions that the requirements don't fully specify.
assertions.evidence: Surfaces three open questions: '1. Availability grouping...distinct dates produce distinct shipments?', '2. Store pickup count...two stores = two shipments?', '3. Warehouse tie-breaking...secondary rule?'

assertions.text: Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules. Acceptable to use a single table only when the domain genuinely has a single concern.
assertions.evidence: Order Split Groups mixes fulfillment type, availability, and delivery address in one 13-row table. Expected output specifies five distinct tables; response provides three with first one combining three concerns.

assertions.text: Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns. Fewer rows per table is expected when concerns are properly separated.
assertions.evidence: Order Split Groups has 13 rows combining fulfillment, availability, and address concerns (e.g. 'All splits in one order'). Combining concerns creates unnecessary permutations that would be eliminated by separate tables.
